etymology: Old English dēad, the state of having life cease. In the New Testament the KJV’s ordinary adjective for corpses and for the spiritually lifeless is Greek nekros (G3498), tagged on the verses below in the verse-cache. The noun-cluster death is treated at the companion entry; this page is the adjective and the company of the dead.
biblical_def: Dead in Scripture is not a metaphor looking for a feeling. It names a real cessation, then uses that cessation as the measure of every lesser death. Physically, the dead are those whose life has ceased: the dead, small and great, stand before God (Rev 20:12), and the dead shall be raised incorruptible (1 Cor 15:52). Spiritually, the unregenerate are dead in trespasses and sins (Eph 2:1) until God quickens them — not nearly-alive, not seeking, not wounded but still climbing, but dead, as Lazarus was dead until the Lord cried come forth. Morally and ecclesiastically, a thing may keep the name of life while being dead: Sardis had a name that thou livest, and art dead (Rev 3:1); faith that will not work is dead, being alone (Jas 2:17); the conscience that still offers the old Levitical round is occupied with dead works (Heb 9:14). Union with Christ adds a fourth use that must not be collapsed into the first three: the believer is to reckon ye also yourselves to be dead indeed unto sin, but alive unto God through Jesus Christ our Lord (Rom 6:11). That death is real — the old man crucified with Christ — and it is not annihilation of the body, nor a mood of self-loathing, but a change of dominion. Christ’s own word holds the whole doctrine together: I am the resurrection, and the life: he that believeth in me, though he were dead, yet shall he live (John 11:25). The dictionary therefore refuses every reading that treats dead as mere poetry. Physical death is the wages of sin; spiritual death is the estate of Adam’s race apart from regenerating grace; the second death is the lake of fire; and the only resurrection unto life is in the Son.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines DEAD as deprived or destitute of life; also, in a state of spiritual death, void of grace, lying under the power of sin; and as the noun, dead men, or the state of the dead.
webster_full: DEAD, a. — Deprived or destitute of life; that state of a being, animal or vegetable, in which the organs of motion and life have ceased to perform their functions. The men are dead who sought thy life (Ex 4:19).

DEAD, a. — In a state of spiritual death; void of grace; lying under the power of sin. Thou hast a name that thou livest, and art dead (Rev 3:1). Not proceeding from spiritual life; not producing good works; as, faith without works is dead (Jas 2:17). Proceeding from corrupt nature; as dead works (Heb 9:14).
DEAD, n. — The dead signifies dead men. Ye shall not make cuttings for the dead (Lev 19:28). Also the state of the dead: This is John the Baptist; he is risen from the dead (Matt 14:2).
scriptures: Ephesians 2:1
And you hath he quickened, who were dead in trespasses and sins;
Romans 6:11
Likewise reckon ye also yourselves to be dead indeed unto sin, but alive unto God through Jesus Christ our Lord.
James 2:17
Even so faith, if it hath not works, is dead, being alone.
Revelation 20:12

And I saw the dead, small and great, stand before God; and the books were opened: and another book was opened, which is the book of life: and the dead were judged out of those things which were written in the books, according to their works.
John 11:25
Jesus said unto her, I am the resurrection, and the life: he that believeth in me, though he were dead, yet shall he live:
corruption_summary: Dead is corrupted when spiritual death is reduced to a mood, when annihilationism erases the second death, when cheap grace calls a fruitless profession living faith, and when death-of-God and therapeutic registers treat the word as style rather than judgment and resurrection.
corruption_paragraphs: The first corruption is to make dead in trespasses and sins mean merely discouraged, unfulfilled, or “dead inside” as an aesthetic. Ephesians 2 is not a wellness diagnosis. It is total inability: the unregenerate man does not cooperate his way into life; God quickens the dead. Semi-Pelagian and decisionist revivalism both refuse this. They need a sinner who is wounded but still climbing. Scripture gives a corpse that only Christ raises.

The second corruption is annihilationism, which denies eternal conscious punishment and therefore empties the dead of Revelation 20. The dead stand; the dead are judged; the second death is not a fade-to-black. Universalism and every scheme that pretends the lake of fire will empty likewise refuse the verdict. The recovery is the creed: bodily resurrection of the just and the unjust, final judgment, heaven for the redeemed, hell for the unredeemed.

The third corruption is a fruitless profession that still claims faith. James does not overthrow justification by faith alone; he names a faith that is not faith — dead, being alone. Rome answers with justifying works. Cheap grace answers with a profession that never obeys. The Reformed confession keeps both ends: the sinner is justified by the imputed righteousness of Christ, received by faith alone; that same faith, being living, works. Sardis is the ecclesiastical form of the same lie: a name that thou livest, and art dead.
roots_summary: Old English dēad. NT adjective in the verses below is Greek nekros (G3498), tagged in the KJV verse-cache at Eph 2:1, Rom 6:11, Jas 2:17, Rev 3:1, Rev 20:12, 1 Cor 15:52. The noun death (Hebrew māwet H4194; Greek thanatos G2288) is the companion entry; this page does not invent further Strong’s numbers beyond those tags and that existing cluster.
roots_lines: Greek nekros (G3498) — dead, a corpse; physically dead and spiritually dead (Eph 2:1; Rom 6:11; Jas 2:17; Rev 3:1; Rev 20:12; 1 Cor 15:52; Matt 8:22).
Greek apothnēskō (G599) — to die; John 11:25, though he were dead, yet shall he live.
Hebrew māwet (H4194) and Greek thanatos (G2288) — death, already treated at the death entry; cited here as the noun-cluster, not as a new number guessed for every OT occurrence of dead.
Old English dēad — destitute of life; the English adjective the KJV uses for both the grave and the unregenerate estate.
usage: Dead in trespasses and sins — spiritual death is inability, not a mood; God quickens the dead.
Dead indeed unto sin, but alive unto God — union with Christ changes dominion; it is not the annihilation of the body.
Faith without works is dead; a church may have a name that it lives and be dead; the dead shall be raised and judged.

etymology: Old English forth, forð: forward, onward, out from confinement into the open. Webster 1828: forward in time; out; into public view. The KJV uses it of creation bringing forth, of the Word going forth, of Lazarus coming forth, of Israel brought forth from Egypt, and of the church going forth unto Christ without the camp.
biblical_def: Forth is the Bible’s small word for a real going-out. God does not leave His works folded in. In the beginning He said, Let the earth bring forth (Gen 1:11), and the earth did. His Word is not a private impression: so shall my word be that goeth forth out of my mouth: it shall not return unto me void (Isa 55:11). The blessed man bringeth forth his fruit in his season (Ps 1:3). Redemption is a bringing-forth: Moses is sent that thou mayest bring forth my people the children of Israel out of Egypt (Ex 3:10). Resurrection is a coming-forth: Jesus cried, Lazarus, come forth (John 11:43), and the dead man came. Discipleship is a going-forth: Let us go forth therefore unto him without the camp, bearing his reproach (Heb 13:13). The adverb therefore traces a single pattern: what God has spoken, planted, redeemed, or raised does not stay inside. It comes out — fruit, people, Word, the living man, the church following a crucified Lord outside the gate. The opposite of forth in this register is not rest; it is the refusal to be sent, the Word left unspoken, the fruit unborne, the camp that will not bear reproach.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines FORTH as forward, onward in time; out; aboard; noting progression from confinement; out into public view or public character.
webster_full: FORTH, adv. — Forward; onward in time; in advance; as from that day forth; from that time forth.
FORTH, adv. — Out; aboard; noting progression or advance from a state of confinement; as, the plants in spring put forth leaves.
FORTH, adv. — Out into public view, or public character. Your country calls you forth into its service.
FORTH, prep. — Out of. (Little used in this construction in modern English; the KJV’s ordinary use is adverbial.)
scriptures: Genesis 1:11
And God said, Let the earth bring forth grass, the herb yielding seed, and the fruit tree yielding fruit after his kind, whose seed is in itself, upon the earth: and it was so.
Isaiah 55:11
So shall my word be that goeth forth out of my mouth: it shall not return unto me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please, and it shall prosper in the thing whereto I sent it.
John 11:43
And when he thus had spoken, he cried with a loud voice, Lazarus, come forth.
Exodus 3:10
Come now therefore, and I will send thee unto Pharaoh, that thou mayest bring forth my people the children of Israel out of Egypt.
Hebrews 13:13
Let us go forth therefore unto him without the camp, bearing his reproach.
corruption_summary: Forth is corrupted when going-out is recast as self-expression (“put yourself out there,” “speak your truth”), when the Word that goes forth is treated as inner voice rather than God’s mouth, and when the church refuses to go forth without the camp because reproach is bad branding.
corruption_paragraphs: Therapeutic and expressive-individualist English has stolen the motion of forth and aimed it at the self. “Put yourself out there.” “Speak your truth.” “Come out” as an identity liturgy. Scripture’s going-forth is not the self arriving on a stage. It is God’s Word leaving His mouth and doing what He sent it to do; it is a people brought out of bondage by His hand; it is a dead man obeying Christ’s cry; it is the church following Jesus outside the gate. The recovery is to restore the subject: God sends; the earth yields; the Word accomplishes; Lazarus comes because He called.

The ecclesiastical form of the corruption is a church that will not go forth without the camp. Hebrews 13 locates Jesus outside the gate, in reproach, and commands the saints to go to Him there. Seeker-sensitive and platform-evangelical instincts reverse the motion: keep the camp comfortable, keep the brand inside the gate, treat reproach as a marketing failure. The apostolic pattern is the opposite. The gospel is preached in all the world (Mark 16:15); the Word goes forth and does not return void; the disciple follows the Lord outside.
roots_summary: Old English forth / forð, forward and out. Verse-cache Strong’s on the quotations below: Hebrew yātsā’ (H3318) at Isa 55:11; Hebrew nāthan (H5414) at Ps 1:3; Greek exō (G1854) at John 11:43 and Heb 13:13; Greek exerchomai (G1831) at Heb 13:13. Genesis 1:11 and Exodus 3:10 are untagged in this cache; no Hebrew number is invented for them.
roots_lines: Hebrew yātsā’ (H3318) — to go out, go forth (Isa 55:11, goeth forth out of my mouth).
Hebrew nāthan (H5414) — to give, put, bring forth (Ps 1:3, bringeth forth his fruit).
Greek exō (G1854) — out, forth, without (John 11:43, come forth; Heb 13:13, without the camp).
Greek exerchomai (G1831) — to go out, go forth (Heb 13:13, Let us go forth).
Old English forth — forward, out from confinement into the open.
usage: Creation, fruit, Word, exodus, resurrection, and discipleship all go forth — God does not leave His works folded in.
Lazarus, come forth is command, not therapy; the dead man comes because Christ called.
Hebrews 13:13 locates the Christian life outside the camp with a reproached Lord, not inside a comfortable brand.

etymology: Old English wiðutan, outside, from without. Webster 1828: not with; in destitution or absence; on the outside of; unless. The KJV uses it for lack (without faith, without shedding of blood), for location (without the camp, without are dogs), and for the old English “outside” (without were fightings, within were fears).
biblical_def: Without in the KJV is first a word of absence, then a word of place. Absence: without faith it is impossible to please him (Heb 11:6); without shedding of blood is no remission (Heb 9:22); without him was not any thing made that was made (John 1:3); the Gentiles were without Christ … having no hope, and without God in the world (Eph 2:12). The grammar is severe. There is no pleasing God in the lack of faith; no remission in the lack of blood; no creation in the lack of the Word; no hope in the lack of Christ. James joins the same preposition to the doctrine of living faith: as the body without the spirit is dead, so faith without works is dead also (Jas 2:26). Place: Jesus suffered without the gate that He might sanctify the people with His own blood, and the church is told to go to Him without the camp (Heb 13:12-13). Revelation closes the holy city with the same adverb of location: without are dogs, and sorcerers, and whoremongers, and murderers, and idolaters, and whosoever loveth and maketh a lie (Rev 22:15). Romans 3:21 must be read in this light and not against it: the righteousness of God without the law is manifested — justification is not earned by the works of the law, which is not permission to live without the law as a rule of life. Without therefore teaches the church what cannot be omitted (faith, blood, Christ, the Spirit’s fruit) and where her Lord stood (outside the gate).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines WITHOUT as not with; in a state of destitution or absence; on the outside of; unless. Adverb: not on the inside; out of doors; externally. Without were fightings, within were fears (2 Cor 7:5).
webster_full: WITHOUT, prep. — Not with; as without success. In a state of destitution or absence from. On the outside of; as without the gate; without doors. Independent of; not by the use of.
WITHOUT, prep. — Unless; except. This use, Webster notes, is nearly superseded by unless and except among good writers, but was common in older English.
WITHOUT, adv. — Not on the inside; not within. Out of doors. Externally; not in the mind. Without were fightings, within were fears (2 Cor 7:5).
scriptures: Hebrews 11:6
But without faith it is impossible to please him: for he that cometh to God must believe that he is, and that he is a rewarder of them that diligently seek him.
Hebrews 9:22
And almost all things are by the law purged with blood; and without shedding of blood is no remission.
John 1:3
All things were made by him; and without him was not any thing made that was made.
James 2:26
For as the body without the spirit is dead, so faith without works is dead also.
Ephesians 2:12
That at that time ye were without Christ, being aliens from the commonwealth of Israel, and strangers from the covenants of promise, having no hope, and without God in the world:
corruption_summary: Without is corrupted by the autonomy that boasts of living without God, without church, without blood, and without law — and by the opposite antinomian misreading of “righteousness without the law” as permission to remain fruitless.
corruption_paragraphs: The age’s favorite use of without is a lifestyle boast: without religion, without rules, without the local church, without the bloody cross. Scripture answers with impossibilities, not options. Without faith it is impossible to please God. Without shedding of blood is no remission. Without Christ the Gentiles were without God in the world. The recovery is to let the preposition do its severe work. What God has named as necessary is not an accessory.

The inverse corruption is antinomian abuse of Romans 3:21. The righteousness of God without the law means justification is not by the works of the law. It does not mean the justified man lives without the law as the rule of gratitude, nor that faith may remain without works. James 2:26 forbids that reading: faith without works is dead. Rome answers James by making works the instrument of justification. Cheap grace answers Paul by making fruit optional. The Reformed confession keeps Paul and James: justified by faith alone, never by a dead faith.
roots_summary: Old English wiðutan, outside / from without. Verse-cache Strong’s on the quotations below: Greek chōris (G5565) at Heb 11:6, Heb 9:22, John 1:3, Jas 2:26, Eph 2:12, Rom 3:21; Greek exō (G1854) at Heb 13:13 and Rev 22:15; Greek exōthen (G1855) at 2 Cor 7:5. No Hebrew number is invented for untagged OT uses.
roots_lines: Greek chōris (G5565) — apart from, without (Heb 11:6; Heb 9:22; John 1:3; Jas 2:26; Eph 2:12; Rom 3:21).
Greek exō (G1854) — outside, without (Heb 13:13, without the camp; Rev 22:15, without are dogs).
Greek exōthen (G1855) — from without, outwardly (2 Cor 7:5, without were fightings).
Old English wiðutan — on the outside; in absence from.
usage: Without faith, without blood, without Christ, without God — Scripture names absences that cannot be survived.
Without the camp is location: Jesus suffered outside the gate; the church goes to Him there.
Romans 3:21 is justification without the works of the law, not a life without obedience; James 2:26 forbids a faith without works.
